'''Amy Catheryne Patterson King''' (December 30, 1928 – June 7, 2014) was an American mathematician and [[mathematics education|mathematics educator]] who became Foundation Professor of mathematics at [[Eastern Kentucky University]], and was recognized for her distinguished teaching by the Kentucky Section of the [[Mathematical Association of America]].

==Personal life==
Amy Catheryne Patterson was born on December 30, 1928, in [[Douglas, Wyoming]]. She married Don King, who became a professor of dentistry;{{r|lhl}} they had no children.{{r|pioneer}} Her brother, James D. Patterson, was also an academic, a professor of physics at the [[Florida Institute of Technology]].{{r|lhl}}

She became a member of the Centenary [[United Methodist Church]] of [[Lexington, Kentucky]]. She died on June 7, 2014, of burns and smoke inhalation from a fire at her home in Lexington.{{r|lhl|pioneer}}

==Education and career==
King was a graduate of the [[University of Missouri]]. She earned a master's degree from [[Wichita State University]]{{r|lhl}} in 1960,{{r|wsu}} with the master's thesis ''Selected methods for solving eigenvalue problems by variational procedures''.{{r|ms}} She joined the [[Mathematical Association of America]] in 1961,{{r|maa}} and coauthored the 1963 book ''Pathways to Probability: History of the Mathematics of Certainty and Chance'' with Cecil Byron Read, published by Holt, Rinehart and Winston.{{r|pathways}} She became a mathematics instructor, including stints at Wichita State University,{{r|lhl}} [[Washburn University]], the [[University of Kansas]], and the [[University of Kentucky]].{{r|scholarship}}

In later life she returned to graduate study,{{r|lhl}} working with [[S. M. Shah]] at the University of Kentucky on [[transcendental function]]s of bounded [[Winding number|index]].{{r|rmj}} She completed her Ph.D. in 1970,{{r|women|phd}} with the dissertation ''A Class of Entire Functions of Bounded Index and Radii of Univalence of Some Functions of Zero Order'' supervised by Shah.{{r|phd}} Her work in the early 1970s also included surveying the contributions of [[women in mathematics]].{{r|women}}

She taught mathematics at Eastern Kentucky University from 1972 until her retirement as Foundation Professor emerita in 1998.{{r|lhl|classroom}}

==Recognition==
King became the inaugural winner of the annual Award for Distinguished College or University Teaching of Mathematics of the Kentucky Section of the [[Mathematical Association of America]], in 1992.{{r|lhl|kymaa}} She was named Foundation Professor at Eastern Kentucky University in 1993;{{r|foundation}} this was "the highest honor the school gives to its teachers".{{r|lhl}} A technology-enhanced mathematics classroom at Eastern Kentucky University was named for her in 2011, honoring her role as a "central figure in mathematics education at EKU".{{r|classroom}}

Wichita State University offers a scholarship named for her,{{r|scholarship}} as does Eastern Kentucky University.{{r|e2pii}}
